“Ship, ahoy! Hast seen the White Whale?”

So cried Ahab, once more hailing a ship showing English colours, bearing down under the stern. Trumpet to mouth, the old man was standing in his hoisted quarter-boat, his ivory leg plainly revealed to the stranger captain, who was carelessly reclining in his own boat’s bow. He was a darkly-tanned, burly, good-natured, fine-looking man, of sixty or thereabouts, dressed in a spacious roundabout, that hung round him in festoons of blue pilot-cloth; and one empty arm of this jacket streamed behind him like the broidered arm of a hussar’s surcoat.
“Hast seen the White Whale?”
“See you this?” and withdrawing it from the folds that had hidden it, he held up a white arm of sperm whale bone, terminating in a wooden head like a mallet.
“Man my boat!” cried Ahab, impetuously, and tossing about the oars near him—“Stand by to lower!”

In less than a minute, without quitting his little craft, he and his crew were dropped to the water, and were soon alongside of the stranger. But here a curious difficulty presented itself. In the excitement of the moment, Ahab had forgotten that since the loss of his leg he had never once stepped on board of any vessel at sea but his own, and then it was always by an ingenious and very handy mechanical contrivance peculiar to the Pequod, and a thing not to be rigged and shipped in any other vessel at a moment’s warning. Now, it is no very easy matter for anybody—except those who are almost hourly used to it, like whalemen—to clamber up a ship’s side from a boat on the open sea; for the great swells now lift the boat high up towards the bulwarks, and then instantaneously drop it half way down to the kelson. So, deprived of one leg, and the strange ship of course being altogether unsupplied with the kindly invention, Ahab now found himself abjectly reduced to a clumsy landsman again; hopelessly eyeing the uncertain changeful height he could hardly hope to attain.

It has before been hinted, perhaps, that every little untoward circumstance that befell him, and which indirectly sprang from his luckless mishap, almost invariably irritated or exasperated Ahab. And in the present instance, all this was heightened by the sight of the two officers of the strange ship, leaning over the side, by the perpendicular ladder of nailed cleets there, and swinging towards him a pair of tastefully-ornamented man-ropes; for at first they did not seem to bethink them that a one-legged man must be too much of a cripple to use their sea bannisters. But this awkwardness only lasted a minute, because the strange captain, observing at a glance how affairs stood, cried out, “I see, I see!—avast heaving there! Jump, boys, and swing over the cutting-tackle.”

As good luck would have it, they had had a whale alongside a day or two previous, and the great tackles were still aloft, and the massive curved blubber-hook, now clean and dry, was still attached to the end. This was quickly lowered to Ahab, who at once comprehending it all, slid his solitary thigh into the curve of the hook (it was like sitting in the fluke of an anchor, or the crotch of an apple tree), and then giving the word, held himself fast, and at the same time also helped to hoist his own weight, by pulling hand-over-hand upon one of the running parts of the tackle. Soon he was carefully swung inside the high bulwarks, and gently landed upon the capstan head. With his ivory arm frankly thrust forth in welcome, the other captain advanced, and Ahab, putting out his ivory leg, and crossing the ivory arm (like two sword-fish blades) cried out in his walrus way, “Aye, aye, hearty! let us shake bones together!—an arm and a leg!—an arm that never can shrink, d’ye see; and a leg that never can run. Where did’st thou see the White Whale?—how long ago?”
“The White Whale,” said the Englishman, pointing his ivory arm towards the East, and taking a rueful sight along it, as if it had been a telescope; “there I saw him, on the Line, last season.”
“And he took that arm off, did he?” asked Ahab, now sliding down from the capstan, and resting on the Englishman’s shoulder, as he did so.
“Aye, he was the cause of it, at least; and that leg, too?”
“Spin me the yarn,” said Ahab; “how was it?”

“It was the first time in my life that I ever cruised on the Line,” began the Englishman. “I was ignorant of the White Whale at that time. Well, one day we lowered for a pod of four or five whales, and my boat fastened to one of them; a regular circus horse he was, too, that went milling and milling round so, that my boat’s crew could only trim dish, by sitting all their sterns on the outer gunwale. Presently up breaches from the bottom of the sea a bouncing great whale, with a milky-white head and hump, all crows’ feet and wrinkles.”
“It was he, it was he!” cried Ahab, suddenly letting out his suspended breath.
“And harpoons sticking in near his starboard fin.”
“Aye, aye—they were mine—my irons,” cried Ahab, exultingly—“but on!”

“Give me a chance, then,” said the Englishman, good-humoredly. “Well, this old great-grandfather, with the white head and hump, runs all afoam into the pod, and goes to snapping furiously at my fast-line!
“Aye, I see!—wanted to part it; free the fast-fish—an old trick—I know him.”

“How it was exactly,” continued the one-armed commander, “I do not know; but in biting the line, it got foul of his teeth, caught there somehow; but we didn’t know it then; so that when we afterwards pulled on the line, bounce we came plump on to his hump! instead of the other whale’s; that went off to windward, all fluking. Seeing how matters stood, and what a noble great whale it was—the noblest and biggest I ever saw, sir, in my life—I resolved to capture him, spite of the boiling rage he seemed to be in. And thinking the hap-hazard line would get loose, or the tooth it was tangled to might draw (for I have a devil of a boat’s crew for a pull on a whale-line); seeing all this, I say, I jumped into my first mate’s boat—Mr. Mounttop’s here (by the way, Captain—Mounttop; Mounttop—the captain);—as I was saying, I jumped into Mounttop’s boat, which, d’ye see, was gunwale and gunwale with mine, then; and snatching the first harpoon, let this old great-grandfather have it. But, Lord, look you, sir—hearts and souls alive, man—the next instant, in a jiff, I was blind as a bat—both eyes out—all befogged and bedeadened with black foam—the whale’s tail looming straight up out of it, perpendicular in the air, like a marble steeple. No use sterning all, then; but as I was groping at midday, with a blinding sun, all crown-jewels; as I was groping, I say, after the second iron, to toss it overboard—down comes the tail like a Lima tower, cutting my boat in two, leaving each half in splinters; and, flukes first, the white hump backed through the wreck, as though it was all chips. We all struck out. To escape his terrible flailings, I seized hold of my harpoon-pole sticking in him, and for a moment clung to that like a sucking fish. But a combing sea dashed me off, and at the same instant, the fish, taking one good dart forwards, went down like a flash; and the barb of that cursed second iron towing along near me caught me here” (clapping his hand just below his shoulder); “yes, caught me just here, I say, and bore me down to Hell’s flames, I was thinking; when, when, all of a sudden, thank the good God, the barb ript its way along the flesh—clear along the whole length of my arm—came out nigh my wrist, and up I floated;—and that gentleman there will tell you the rest (by the way, captain—Dr. Bunger, ship’s surgeon: Bunger, my lad,—the captain). Now, Bunger boy, spin your part of the yarn.”

The professional gentleman thus familiarly pointed out, had been all the time standing near them, with nothing specific visible, to denote his gentlemanly rank on board. His face was an exceedingly round but sober one; he was dressed in a faded blue woollen frock or shirt, and patched trowsers; and had thus far been dividing his attention between a marlingspike he held in one hand, and a pill-box held in the other, occasionally casting a critical glance at the ivory limbs of the two crippled captains. But, at his superior’s introduction of him to Ahab, he politely bowed, and straightway went on to do his captain’s bidding.
“It was a shocking bad wound,” began the whale-surgeon; “and, taking my advice, Captain Boomer here, stood our old Sammy—”
“Samuel Enderby is the name of my ship,” interrupted the one-armed captain, addressing Ahab; “go on, boy.”

“Stood our old Sammy off to the northward, to get out of the blazing hot weather there on the Line. But it was no use—I did all I could; sat up with him nights; was very severe with him in the matter of diet—”

“Oh, very severe!” chimed in the patient himself; then suddenly altering his voice, “Drinking hot rum toddies with me every night, till he couldn’t see to put on the bandages; and sending me to bed, half seas over, about three o’clock in the morning. Oh, ye stars! he sat up with me indeed, and was very severe in my diet. Oh! a great watcher, and very dietetically severe, is Dr. Bunger. (Bunger, you dog, laugh out! why don’t ye? You know you’re a precious jolly rascal.) But, heave ahead, boy, I’d rather be killed by you than kept alive by any other man.”

“My captain, you must have ere this perceived, respected sir”—said the imperturbable godly-looking Bunger, slightly bowing to Ahab—“is apt to be facetious at times; he spins us many clever things of that sort. But I may as well say—en passant, as the French remark—that I myself—that is to say, Jack Bunger, late of the reverend clergy—am a strict total abstinence man; I never drink—”
“Water!” cried the captain; “he never drinks it; it’s a sort of fits to him; fresh water throws him into the hydrophobia; but go on—go on with the arm story.”

“Yes, I may as well,” said the surgeon, coolly. “I was about observing, sir, before Captain Boomer’s facetious interruption, that spite of my best and severest endeavors, the wound kept getting worse and worse; the truth was, sir, it was as ugly gaping wound as surgeon ever saw; more than two feet and several inches long. I measured it with the lead line. In short, it grew black; I knew what was threatened, and off it came. But I had no hand in shipping that ivory arm there; that thing is against all rule”—pointing at it with the marlingspike—“that is the captain’s work, not mine; he ordered the carpenter to make it; he had that club-hammer there put to the end, to knock some one’s brains out with, I suppose, as he tried mine once. He flies into diabolical passions sometimes. Do ye see this dent, sir”—removing his hat, and brushing aside his hair, and exposing a bowl-like cavity in his skull, but which bore not the slightest scarry trace, or any token of ever having been a wound—“Well, the captain there will tell you how that came here; he knows.”

“No, I don’t,” said the captain, “but his mother did; he was born with it. Oh, you solemn rogue, you—you Bunger! was there ever such another Bunger in the watery world? Bunger, when you die, you ought to die in pickle, you dog; you should be preserved to future ages, you rascal.”
“What became of the White Whale?” now cried Ahab, who thus far had been impatiently listening to this by-play between the two Englishmen.

“Oh!” cried the one-armed captain, “oh, yes! Well; after he sounded, we didn’t see him again for some time; in fact, as I before hinted, I didn’t then know what whale it was that had served me such a trick, till some time afterwards, when coming back to the Line, we heard about Moby Dick—as some call him—and then I knew it was he.”

“Twice.”
“But could not fasten?”
“Didn’t want to try to: ain’t one limb enough? What should I do without this other arm? And I’m thinking Moby Dick doesn’t bite so much as he swallows.”

“Well, then,” interrupted Bunger, “give him your left arm for bait to get the right. Do you know, gentlemen”—very gravely and mathematically bowing to each Captain in succession—“Do you know, gentlemen, that the digestive organs of the whale are so inscrutably constructed by Divine Providence, that it is quite impossible for him to completely digest even a man’s arm? And he knows it too. So that what you take for the White Whale’s malice is only his awkwardness. For he never means to swallow a single limb; he only thinks to terrify by feints. But sometimes he is like the old juggling fellow, formerly a patient of mine in Ceylon, that making believe swallow jack-knives, once upon a time let one drop into him in good earnest, and there it stayed for a twelvemonth or more; when I gave him an emetic, and he heaved it up in small tacks, d’ye see. No possible way for him to digest that jack-knife, and fully incorporate it into his general bodily system. Yes, Captain Boomer, if you are quick enough about it, and have a mind to pawn one arm for the sake of the privilege of giving decent burial to the other, why in that case the arm is yours; only let the whale have another chance at you shortly, that’s all.”

“No, thank ye, Bunger,” said the English Captain, “he’s welcome to the arm he has, since I can’t help it, and didn’t know him then; but not to another one. No more White Whales for me; I’ve lowered for him once, and that has satisfied me. There would be great glory in killing him, I know that; and there is a ship-load of precious sperm in him, but, hark ye, he’s best let alone; don’t you think so, Captain?”—glancing at the ivory leg.

“He is. But he will still be hunted, for all that. What is best let alone, that accursed thing is not always what least allures. He’s all a magnet! How long since thou saw’st him last? Which way heading?”

“Bless my soul, and curse the foul fiend’s,” cried Bunger, stoopingly walking round Ahab, and like a dog, strangely snuffing; “this man’s blood—bring the thermometer!—it’s at the boiling point!—his pulse makes these planks beat!—sir!”—taking a lancet from his pocket, and drawing near to Ahab’s arm.
“Avast!” roared Ahab, dashing him against the bulwarks—“Man the boat! Which way heading?”
“Good God!” cried the English Captain, to whom the question was put. “What’s the matter? He was heading east, I think.—Is your Captain crazy?” whispering Fedallah.

But Fedallah, putting a finger on his lip, slid over the bulwarks to take the boat’s steering oar, and Ahab, swinging the cutting-tackle towards him, commanded the ship’s sailors to stand by to lower.

Ahab shouted this as he hailed yet another ship, this one flying English colors and bearing down under the stern. The old man stood in his hoisted quarter-boat with the trumpet to his mouth, his ivory leg in plain view of the stranger captain, who was lounging casually in the bow of his own boat. He was a deeply tanned, burly, good-natured, handsome man of about sixty, dressed in a roomy short jacket that hung around him in folds of blue pilot-cloth; one empty sleeve of it streamed out behind him like the embroidered sleeve of a hussar's cloak.
"Have you seen the White Whale?"
"Do you see this?" From the folds that had hidden it, he drew out a white arm made of sperm whale bone, ending in a wooden head like a mallet, and held it up.
"Man my boat!" cried Ahab, impetuously tossing about the oars near him. "Stand by to lower!"

In less than a minute Ahab and his crew, still sitting in their little boat, had been lowered to the water, and they were soon alongside the stranger. But now an odd problem came up. In the excitement of the moment Ahab had forgotten that since losing his leg he had never once boarded any ship at sea except his own, and even then always by means of a clever and very handy mechanical device found only on the Pequod, which could not be rigged up and fitted on another vessel at a moment's notice. Now, it is not at all easy for anyone except people who do it almost every hour, like whalemen, to climb up a ship's side from a boat on the open sea, because the great swells lift the boat high up toward the bulwarks one moment and in the next instant drop it halfway down to the keelson. So, with one leg gone, and the strange ship naturally having none of that thoughtful invention, Ahab found himself miserably reduced to a clumsy landsman again, staring hopelessly at the shifting, uncertain height he could hardly hope to climb.

I may have hinted before that almost every small mishap that came his way as an indirect result of his unlucky injury irritated or infuriated Ahab. This time all of that was made worse by the sight of the strange ship's two officers leaning over the side next to the upright ladder of nailed-on cleats and swinging a pair of prettily decorated man-ropes toward him; at first it did not seem to occur to them that a one-legged man would be too crippled to use their sea-banisters. But this awkward moment lasted only a minute, because the strange captain saw at a glance how things stood and called out, "I see, I see! Stop hauling there! Jump to it, boys, and swing over the cutting-tackle."

As good luck would have it, they had had a whale alongside a day or two before, and the great tackles were still aloft, and the massive curved blubber-hook, now clean and dry, was still attached to the end. This was quickly lowered to Ahab, who at once understanding everything, slid his solitary thigh into the curve of the hook — it was like sitting in the fluke of an anchor, or the crotch of an apple tree — and then giving the word, held himself fast while also helping to hoist his own weight by pulling hand-over-hand upon one of the running parts of the tackle. Soon he was carefully swung inside the high bulwarks and gently landed upon the capstan head. With his ivory arm frankly thrust forth in welcome, the other captain advanced, and Ahab, putting out his ivory leg and crossing the ivory arm — like two swordfish blades — cried out in his walrus way: "Aye, aye, hearty! Let us shake bones together! An arm and a leg! An arm that never can shrink, d'you see, and a leg that never can run. Where did you see the White Whale? How long ago?"

"The White Whale," said the Englishman, pointing his ivory arm toward the east and taking a rueful sight along it as if it had been a telescope, "there I saw him, on the Line (the equator), last season."
"And he took that arm off, did he?" asked Ahab, now sliding down from the capstan and resting on the Englishman's shoulder as he did so.
"Aye, he was the cause of it, at least. And that leg, too?"
"Spin me the yarn," said Ahab. "How was it?"

"It was the first time in my life I had ever cruised on the Line," the Englishman began. "I didn't know anything about the White Whale back then. Well, one day we lowered for a pod of four or five whales, and my boat got fast to one of them. He was a real circus horse, too, going round and round in circles, so that the only way my boat's crew could keep her level was by all sitting with their backsides on the outer gunwale. Then all of a sudden a great bouncing whale comes breaching up from the bottom of the sea, with a milky-white head and hump, all crow's-feet and wrinkles."
"It was he, it was he!" cried Ahab, suddenly letting out his suspended breath.
"And harpoons sticking in near his starboard fin."
"Aye, aye — they were mine — my irons," cried Ahab, exultantly — "but go on!"

"Give me a chance, then," said the Englishman, good-humoredly. "Well, this old great-grandfather, with the white head and hump, runs all foaming into the pod and goes to snapping furiously at my fast-line!"
"Aye, I see! Wanted to part it — free the fast-fish — an old trick — I know him."

"How it was exactly," continued the one-armed commander, "I do not know. But in biting the line, it got foul of his teeth, caught there somehow. But we didn't know it then, so that when we afterward pulled on the line, bounce we came plump onto his hump! — instead of the other whale's, that went off to windward, all fluking. Seeing how matters stood, and what a noble great whale it was — the noblest and biggest I ever saw, sir, in my life — I resolved to capture him, despite the boiling rage he seemed to be in. And thinking the tangled line would get loose, or the tooth it was caught on might pull free — for I have a devil of a boat's crew for a pull on a whale-line — seeing all this, I say, I jumped into my first mate's boat. Mr. Mounttop's here — by the way, Captain: Mounttop; Mounttop: the Captain. As I was saying, I jumped into Mounttop's boat, which was gunwale to gunwale with mine then, and snatching the first harpoon, let this old great-grandfather have it. But Lord, look you, sir — hearts and souls alive, man — the next instant, in a flash, I was blind as a bat — both eyes out — all befogged and bedeadened with black foam, the whale's tail looming straight up out of it, perpendicular in the air like a marble steeple. No use backing off then. But as I was groping at midday with a blinding sun, all crown-jewels — as I was groping, I say, after the second iron to toss it overboard — down comes the tail like a Lima tower, cutting my boat in two, leaving each half in splinters. And, flukes first, the white hump backed through the wreck as though it was all chips. We all struck out. To escape his terrible flailing, I seized hold of my harpoon-pole sticking in him and for a moment clung to that like a sucker-fish. But a breaking wave dashed me off, and at the same instant the fish, taking one good dart forward, went down like a flash. And the barb of that cursed second iron, towing along near me, caught me here" — clapping his hand just below his shoulder — "yes, caught me just here, I say, and bore me down to Hell's flames, I was thinking. When — when — all of a sudden, thank the good God, the barb ripped its way along the flesh — clear along the whole length of my arm — came out near my wrist, and up I floated. And that gentleman there will tell you the rest. By the way, Captain: Dr. Bunger, ship's surgeon; Bunger, my lad: the Captain. Now, Bunger boy, spin your part of the yarn."

The professional gentleman being pointed out so casually had been standing near them the whole time, with nothing in particular to show his gentleman's rank on board. His face was extremely round but serious. He wore a faded blue woolen frock, or shirt, and patched trousers, and until now he had been dividing his attention between a marlinspike in one hand and a pill-box in the other, now and then throwing a critical glance at the ivory limbs of the two crippled captains. But when his superior introduced him to Ahab, he bowed politely and went straight off to do what his captain had asked.
"It was a shockingly bad wound," began the whale-surgeon, "and taking my advice, Captain Boomer here stood our old Sammy —"
"Samuel Enderby is the name of my ship," interrupted the one-armed captain, addressing Ahab. "Go on, boy."

"Stood our old Sammy off to the northward, to get out of the blazing hot weather there on the Line. But it was no use — I did all I could; sat up with him nights; was very severe with him about his diet —"

"Oh, very severe!" chimed in the patient himself. Then suddenly changing his tone: "Drinking hot rum toddies with me every night till he couldn't see to put on the bandages, and sending me to bed, half-drunk, about three o'clock in the morning. Oh, you stars! He sat up with me indeed, and was very severe with my diet. Oh, a great watcher and very dietetically severe is Dr. Bunger. — Bunger, you dog, laugh out! Why don't you? You know you're a precious jolly rascal. — But push ahead, boy. I'd rather be killed by you than kept alive by any other man."

"My captain, you must have by now perceived, respected sir" — said the unflappable, pious-looking Bunger, slightly bowing to Ahab — "is inclined to be humorous at times. He spins us many clever things of that sort. But I may as well say — en passant, as the French remark — that I myself — that is to say, Jack Bunger, late of the reverend clergy — am a strict total abstinence man. I never drink —"
"Water!" cried the captain. "He never drinks it. It gives him a sort of fits. Fresh water throws him into the hydrophobia. But go on — go on with the arm story."

"Yes, I may as well," said the surgeon, coolly. "I was about to observe, sir, before Captain Boomer's humorous interruption, that despite my best and severest efforts, the wound kept getting worse and worse. The truth was, sir, it was as ugly a gaping wound as surgeon ever saw — more than two feet and several inches long. I measured it with the lead line. In short, it turned black. I knew what was threatened, and off it came. But I had no hand in shipping that ivory arm there" — pointing at it with the marlinspike — "that thing is against all rule. That is the captain's work, not mine. He ordered the carpenter to make it. He had that club-hammer there put on the end to knock someone's brains out with, I suppose, as he tried mine once. He flies into diabolical rages sometimes. Do you see this dent, sir?" — removing his hat and brushing aside his hair, exposing a bowl-like cavity in his skull, but which bore not the slightest scar or any token of ever having been a wound — "Well, the captain there will tell you how that came to be. He knows."

"No, I don't," said the captain, "but his mother did; he was born with it. Oh, you solemn rogue, you — you Bunger! Was there ever such another Bunger in the watery world? Bunger, when you die, you ought to die in pickle, you dog. You should be preserved for future ages, you rascal."
"What happened to the White Whale?" Ahab shouted now; up to this point he had been listening impatiently to this byplay between the two Englishmen.

"Oh!" cried the one-armed captain. "Oh, yes! Well, after he sounded, we didn't see him again for some time. In fact, as I hinted before, I didn't then know what whale it was that had served me such a trick, till some time afterward, when coming back to the Line, we heard about Moby Dick — as some call him — and then I knew it was he."
"Did you cross his wake again?"
"Twice."
"But could not fasten?"
"Didn't want to try. Ain't one limb enough? What should I do without this other arm? And I'm thinking Moby Dick doesn't bite so much as he swallows."

"Well, then," Bunger broke in, "give him your left arm as bait to get back the right. Do you know, gentlemen" — bowing very gravely and with mathematical precision to each captain in turn — "do you know, gentlemen, that Divine Providence has built the whale's digestive organs so mysteriously that he cannot possibly digest even a man's arm completely? And he knows it, too. So what you take for the White Whale's malice is only his clumsiness. He never intends to swallow a single limb; he only means to scare you with feints. But sometimes he is like the old juggler, once a patient of mine in Ceylon, who used to pretend to swallow jackknives, and one day actually let one slip down inside him for real. There it stayed for a year or more, until I gave him an emetic and he threw it up in little tacks, you see. There was no possible way for him to digest that jackknife and fully absorb it into his general bodily system. Yes, Captain Boomer, if you are quick enough about it, and are willing to pawn one arm for the privilege of giving the other a decent burial, why, in that case the arm is yours. Just let the whale have another go at you soon, that's all."

"No, thank you, Bunger," said the English captain. "He's welcome to the arm he has, since I can't help it and didn't know him then. But not to another one. No more White Whales for me. I've lowered for him once, and that has satisfied me. There would be great glory in killing him, I know that, and there is a shipload of precious sperm in him. But hark you, he's best let alone. Don't you think so, Captain?" — glancing at the ivory leg.

"He is. But he will still be hunted, for all that. The accursed thing that is best let alone is not always the thing that least allures. He's all a magnet! How long since you saw him last? Which way heading?"

"Bless my soul, and curse the foul fiend's," cried Bunger, stooping and walking round Ahab, and like a dog strangely sniffing, "this man's blood — bring the thermometer! — it's at the boiling point! His pulse makes these planks beat! Sir!" — taking a lancet from his pocket and drawing near to Ahab's arm.
"Back off!" roared Ahab, dashing him against the bulwarks. "Man the boat! Which way heading?"
"Good God!" cried the English captain, to whom the question was put. "What's the matter? He was heading east, I think. Is your captain crazy?" whispering to Fedallah.

But Fedallah put a finger to his lips and slid over the bulwarks to take the boat's steering oar, while Ahab swung the cutting-tackle over to himself and ordered the ship's sailors to get ready to lower.

A moment later he was standing in the stern of the boat, and the Manila men were jumping to their oars. The English captain called after him, but it was no use. Ahab stood upright, his back to the stranger ship and his face set like flint toward his own, until they came alongside the Pequod.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 100 — Ben og arm
paragraphs: Pequod fra Nantucket mødes med Samuel Enderby fra London.
»Skib ohøj! Har I set den hvide hval?«

Det råbte Ahab, da han anråbte endnu et skib, et med engelske farver, der kom sejlende ned mod agterenden af Pequod. Den gamle mand stod i sin ophejste agterbåd med råberen for munden, så hans elfenbensben var tydeligt at se for den fremmede kaptajn, som lå og hvilede sig i det fri i stævnen på sin egen båd. Han var en dybt solbrændt, kraftig, godmodig og køn mand på omkring tres, iført en rummelig kort jakke i blåt lodsklæde, som hang i folder omkring ham. Det ene tomme ærme flagrede bag ham som det broderede ærme på en husarkappe.
»Har I set den hvide hval?«
»Ser I det her?« Fra foldene, der havde skjult den, trak han en hvid arm af kaskelotknogle frem, som endte i et træhoved som en køllehammer, og holdt den op.
»Bemand min båd!« råbte Ahab og smed hidsigt rundt med årerne ved siden af sig. »Gør klar til at sænke!«

På under et minut var Ahab og hans mandskab, der stadig sad i deres lille båd, blevet firet ned i vandet, og snart lå de langs siden af den fremmede. Men nu opstod der et besynderligt problem. I øjeblikkets ophidselse havde Ahab glemt, at han lige siden han mistede sit ben aldrig én eneste gang var kommet om bord på noget skib på havet bortset fra sit eget, og selv dér altid ved hjælp af en snedig og meget praktisk mekanisk indretning, som kun fandtes på Pequod, og som ikke kunne rigges til og sættes op på et andet skib med et øjebliks varsel. Nu er det slet ikke let for andre end folk, der gør det næsten hver time, som hvalfangere, at klatre op ad et skibs side fra en båd på åbent hav, for de store dønninger løfter båden højt op mod essingerne i det ene øjeblik og lader den falde halvvejs ned til kølsvinet i det næste. Så med det ene ben væk, og med det fremmede skib, der naturligvis ikke havde noget af den omsigtige opfindelse, så Ahab sig ynkeligt gjort til en klodset landkrabbe igen. Håbløst stirrede han op på den skiftende, usikre højde, som han næppe kunne håbe at komme op ad.

Jeg har måske antydet før, at næsten hvert eneste lille uheld, der ramte ham som en indirekte følge af hans uheldige skade, irriterede eller gjorde Ahab rasende. Denne gang blev det hele gjort værre af at se det fremmede skibs to officerer læne sig ud over rælingen ved siden af den lodrette stige af påsømmede trin og svinge et par smukt pyntede mandreb ud mod ham. Først faldt det dem ikke ind, at en enbenet mand ville være for forkrøblet til at bruge deres søgelændere. Men det pinlige øjeblik varede kun et minut, for den fremmede kaptajn så med det samme, hvordan landet lå, og råbte: »Jeg ser det, jeg ser det! Hold op med at hale dér! Af sted med jer, drenge, og sving skæretaljen herover.«

Heldigvis havde de haft en hval langs siden en dag eller to før, så de store taljer hang stadig oppe, og den vældige, krumme flensekrog, nu ren og tør, sad stadig for enden. Den blev hurtigt firet ned til Ahab, som med det samme forstod det hele og lod sit eneste lår glide ind i krogens bugt — det var som at sidde i et ankers fluke eller i gaflen på et æbletræ — og så gav han signal og holdt sig fast, mens han også hjalp med at hejse sin egen vægt ved at hale hånd over hånd i en af taljens løbende parter. Snart blev han forsigtigt svunget ind over den høje ræling og sat blidt ned på gangspillets hoved. Den anden kaptajn kom frem med sin elfenbensarm åbent rakt frem som velkomst, og Ahab stak sit elfenbensben ud og krydsede det med elfenbensarmen — som to sværdfiskesværd — og råbte på sin hvalrosagtige måde: »Ja, ja, gamle ven! Lad os trykke knogler! En arm og et ben! En arm, der aldrig kan krympe sig, forstår du, og et ben, der aldrig kan løbe sin vej. Hvor så du den hvide hval? Hvor længe siden?«
»Den hvide hval,« sagde englænderen og pegede med sin elfenbensarm mod øst og pejlede sorgfuldt langs den, som om den var en kikkert, »dér så jeg ham, ved Linjen (ækvator), sidste sæson.«
»Og det var ham, der tog den arm, ikke sandt?« spurgte Ahab og gled nu ned fra gangspillet og hvilede på englænderens skulder, mens han gjorde det.
»Ja, han var i hvert fald skyld i det. Og det ben, også?«
»Spin mig historien,« sagde Ahab. »Hvordan gik det til?«

»Det var første gang i mit liv, jeg krydsede på Linjen,« begyndte englænderen. »Jeg vidste ikke noget som helst om den hvide hval dengang. Nå, en dag sænkede vi efter en flok på fire-fem hvaler, og min båd kom fast i en af dem. Han var sandelig en cirkushest, for han gik rundt og rundt i ring, så den eneste måde, min bådsbesætning kunne holde den i ligevægt, var ved at sidde med numsen på den yderste essing. Så pludselig kommer en vældig, hoppende hval brydende op fra havets bund med et mælkehvidt hoved og pukkel, helt fuld af kragetæer og rynker.«
»Det var ham, det var ham!« råbte Ahab og lod pludselig sit tilbageholdte åndedræt slippe ud.
»Og harpuner siddende nær hans styrbords finne.«
»Ja, ja — de var mine — mine jern,« råbte Ahab jublende — »men fortsæt!«
»Giv mig tid, så,« sagde englænderen godmodigt. »Nå, den gamle oldefar med det hvide hoved og puklen går skummende lige ind i flokken og begynder at bide rasende i min fangline!«
»Ja, jeg ser det! Ville slide den over — løslade den fastholdte hval — et gammelt kneb — jeg kender ham.«

»Hvordan det helt præcist gik til,« fortsatte den enarmede kaptajn, »ved jeg ikke. Men da han bed i linen, kom den i klemme på hans tænder og satte sig fast dér på en eller anden måde. Men det vidste vi ikke dengang, så da vi bagefter halede i linen, røg vi bums lige op på hans pukkel! — i stedet for den anden hvals, der drog af sted til luvart og slog med halen. Da jeg så, hvordan det stod til, og hvilken ædel stor hval det var — den ædleste og største, jeg nogensinde har set, sir, i mit liv — besluttede jeg at fange ham, trods det kogende raseri, han syntes at være i. Og i den tro, at den filtrede line ville gå løs, eller at tanden, den sad fast på, ville give slip — for jeg har en djævelsk bådsbesætning til at hale i en hvallinje — da jeg altså så alt dette, sprang jeg over i min første styrmands båd. Mr. Mounttop er her — forresten, kaptajn: Mounttop; Mounttop: kaptajnen. Som jeg sagde, sprang jeg over i Mounttops båd, som dengang lå essing mod essing med min, og greb den første harpun og gav den gamle oldefar den. Men Herregud, forstår I, sir — hjerter og sjæle, mand — i næste øjeblik, i et lyn, var jeg blind som en flagermus — begge øjne ude — alt omtåget og døvet af sort skum, og hvalens hale rejste sig lige op af det, lodret i luften som et marmortårn. Det nyttede ikke at bakke væk nu. Men mens jeg famlede ved højlys dag i en blændende sol, fuld af kronjuveler — mens jeg famlede, siger jeg, efter det andet jern for at smide det over bord — kommer halen ned som et tårn i Lima og skærer min båd over i to og efterlader hver halvdel i splinter. Og med halen først bakkede den hvide pukkel gennem vraget, som om det kun var spåner. Vi svømmede alle for livet. For at slippe for hans frygtelige slag greb jeg fat i mit harpunskaft, der sad i ham, og klamrede mig et øjeblik til den som en sugefisk. Men en brydende bølge kastede mig af, og i samme øjeblik slog fisken et godt skud fremad og gik ned som et lyn. Og modhagen på det forbandede andet jern, som slæbte hen nær mig, fik fat i mig her« — og han slog hånden lige under skulderen — »ja, fik fat i mig lige her, siger jeg, og trak mig ned til Helvedes flammer, tænkte jeg. Da — da — pludselig, Gud ske tak og lov, flåede modhagen sig vej gennem kødet — langs hele min arms længde — og kom ud nær håndleddet, og op fløt jeg. Og den herre dér kan fortælle jer resten. Forresten, kaptajn: doktor Bunger, skibets læge; Bunger, min dreng: kaptajnen. Nu, Bunger, gamle dreng, spin din del af historien.«

Den professionelle herre, der således så uformelt blev peget ud, havde stået tæt ved dem hele tiden uden noget særligt, der viste hans herrerang om bord. Hans ansigt var ekstremt rundt, men alvorligt. Han bar en falmet blå uldkittel eller skjorte og lappede bukser, og indtil nu havde han delt sin opmærksomhed mellem en marlepig i den ene hånd og en pilleæske i den anden, mens han nu og da kastede et kritisk blik på de to forkrøblede kaptajners elfenbensdele. Men da hans foresatte præsenterede ham for Ahab, bukkede han høfligt og gik straks i gang med at gøre, hvad hans kaptajn havde bedt om.
»Det var et skrækkeligt slemt sår,« begyndte hvallægen, »og på mit råd satte kaptajn Boomer her kursen for vores gamle Sammy —«
»Samuel Enderby er mit skibs navn,« afbrød den enarmede kaptajn og vendte sig til Ahab. »Fortsæt, dreng.«

»Nordpå, for at komme væk fra det brændende hede vejr dernede ved Linjen. Men det nyttede ikke — jeg gjorde alt, hvad jeg kunne; sad oppe hos ham om natten; var meget streng over for ham med hensyn til hans kost —«

»Å, meget streng!« indskød patienten selv. Så skiftede han pludselig tone: »Drak varm romgrog med mig hver eneste nat, til han ikke kunne se at lægge forbindingerne på, og sendte mig i seng halvfuld ved tre-tiden om morgenen. Å, I stjerner! Han sad oppe hos mig, ja, og var meget streng med min kost. Å, en stor nattevagt og meget diætetisk streng er doktor Bunger. — Bunger, din hund, grin højt! Hvorfor gør du ikke det? Du ved godt, du er en gevaldig lystig slubbert. — Men kør på, dreng. Jeg vil hellere blive dræbt af dig end holdt i live af nogen anden mand.«

»Min kaptajn har nu sikkert bemærket, ærede sir,« — sagde den uforstyrrelige, fromt udseende Bunger og bukkede let for Ahab — »er tilbøjelig til at være morsom til tider. Han spinder mange kloge ting af den slags for os. Men jeg kan lige så godt sige — en passant, som franskmændene siger — at jeg selv — det vil sige, Jack Bunger, tidligere af den ærværdige præstestand — er en strengt afholdende mand. Jeg drikker aldrig —«
»Vand!« råbte kaptajnen. »Det drikker han aldrig. Det giver ham en slags anfald. Ferskvand sætter ham i vandskræk. Men fortsæt — fortsæt med armhistorien.«

»Ja, det kan jeg lige så godt,« sagde lægen køligt. »Jeg var ved at bemærke, sir, før kaptajn Boomers morsomme afbrydelse, at trods min bedste og strengeste indsats blev såret værre og værre. Sandheden var, sir, at det var et så grimt gabende sår, som nogen læge har set — mere end to fod og adskillige tommer langt. Jeg målte det med lodlinen. Kort sagt, det blev sort. Jeg vidste, hvad der truede, og af kom den. Men jeg havde ingen hånd i at skaffe den elfenbensarm dér« — og han pegede på den med marlepigen — »den ting er imod alle regler. Det er kaptajnens værk, ikke mit. Han bad tømreren om at lave den. Han fik den køllehammer dér sat på enden for at slå hjernen ud på nogen med, formoder jeg, som han engang prøvede på min. Han flyver nogle gange ud i djævelsk raseri. Ser I den her bule, sir?« — og han tog hatten af og strøg håret til side og viste en skålformet fordybning i kraniet, men som ikke bar det mindste ar eller tegn på nogensinde at have været et sår — »Nå, kaptajnen dér kan fortælle jer, hvordan det kom til. Han ved det.«

»Nej, det gør jeg ikke,« sagde kaptajnen, »men hans mor gjorde; han blev født med det. Å, din højtidelige slyngel, din — din Bunger! Fandtes der nogensinde en anden Bunger som ham i den vandige verden? Bunger, når du dør, bør du dø i saltlage, din hund. Du bør bevares for kommende tidsaldre, din slubbert.«
»Hvad skete der med den hvide hval?« råbte Ahab nu; indtil da havde han utålmodigt lyttet til denne ordveksling mellem de to englændere.

»Å!« råbte den enarmede kaptajn. »Å, ja! Nå, efter at han var dykket, så vi ham ikke igen i nogen tid. Faktisk, som jeg antydede før, vidste jeg ikke dengang, hvilken hval det var, der havde spillet mig sådan et puds, først nogen tid senere, da vi vendte tilbage til Linjen og hørte om Moby Dick — som nogle kalder ham — og da vidste jeg, at det var ham.«
»Krydsede I hans kølvand igen?«
»To gange.«
»Men kunne ikke få fast i ham?«
»Gad ikke prøve. Er ét lem ikke nok? Hvad skulle jeg gøre uden denne anden arm? Og jeg tænker, at Moby Dick ikke bider så meget, som han sluger.«

»Nå, så,« faldt Bunger ind, »giv ham din venstre arm som lokkemad for at få den højre tilbage. Ved I hvad, mine herrer« — og han bukkede meget alvorligt og med matematisk nøjagtighed for hver af kaptajnerne i tur og orden — »ved I, mine herrer, at Guds forsyn har bygget hvalens fordøjelsesorganer så mystisk, at han umuligt kan fordøje selv en mands arm helt? Og han ved det også. Så det, I tager for den hvide hvals ondskab, er blot hans klodsethed. Han har aldrig til hensigt at sluge et eneste lem; han vil kun skræmme jer med skinmanøvrer. Men nogle gange er han som den gamle gøgler, engang en patient af mig på Ceylon, som plejede at lade, som om han slugte lommeknive, og en dag virkelig lod en glide ned i sig. Dér blev den i et år eller mere, indtil jeg gav ham et brækmiddel, og han kastede den op i små stifter, ser I. Der var ingen mulig måde, hvorpå han kunne fordøje den lommekniv og få den helt optaget i sit almindelige legeme. Ja, kaptajn Boomer, hvis du er hurtig nok til det og er villig til at pantsætte den ene arm for privilegiet at give den anden en ordentlig begravelse, ja, så er armen din. Lad bare hvalen give sig i kast med dig igen snart, det er det hele.«

»Nej tak, Bunger,« sagde den engelske kaptajn. »Han er velkommen til den arm, han har, for jeg kan ikke gøre det ugjort, og dengang kendte jeg ham ikke. Men ikke til endnu en. Ikke flere hvide hvaler for mig. Jeg har sat både i vandet efter ham én gang, og det har været nok. Der ville være stor ære i at dræbe ham, det ved jeg, og der er en hel skibsladning dyrebar spermolie i ham. Men hør her, det er bedst at lade ham være. Synes du ikke også det, kaptajn?« — og han kastede et blik på elfenbensbenet.

»Jo, det er det. Men han bliver alligevel jagtet, uanset hvad. Den forbandede ting, det er bedst at lade være, er ikke altid den, der lokker mindst. Han er rent ud sagt én stor magnet! Hvor længe er det siden, du så ham sidst? Hvilken vej sejlede han?«

»Du milde! Og pokker i vold med fandens...« råbte Bunger, mens han bøjede sig og gik rundt om Ahab og snusede mærkeligt som en hund. »Den mands blod — hent termometret! — det er ved kogepunktet! Hans puls får dækket til at banke! Sir!« — og han tog en lancet op af lommen og nærmede sig Ahabs arm.
»Af med dig!« brølede Ahab og slyngede ham mod rælingen. »Bemand båden! Hvilken vej sejlede han?«
»Du gode Gud!« råbte den engelske kaptajn, som spørgsmålet var stillet til. »Hvad er der i vejen? Han sejlede mod øst, tror jeg. Er jeres kaptajn gal?« hviskede han til Fedallah.

Men Fedallah lagde en finger på læberne og gled over rælingen for at tage styreåren i båden, mens Ahab svang skæretaljen over til sig og befalede skibets matroser at gøre klar til at sætte bådene i vandet.

Et øjeblik efter stod han i båden agter, og manilamændene sprang til årerne. Den engelske kaptajn råbte efter ham, men det nyttede ikke. Ahab stod rank med ryggen mod det fremmede skib og ansigtet sat som flint mod sit eget, indtil de lå langs med Pequod.
